newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean computer chip makers gamble on profits.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean computer chip makers gamble on profits.

text.p: South Korea's Samsung Electronics said on Thursday it would further curb output of 16-megabit computer memory chips in what some analysts saw as a gamble to shift the global market towards higher-value chips.

Samsung is the world's largest producer of 16-megabit dynamic random access memory chips (DRAMs), whose price has been in freefall for a year, slashing corporate profits and damaging Asian economies heavily reliant on exports of semiconducters.
On Wednesday another South Korean electronics giant, Lg Semicon, said it would shift away from producing 16-megabit chips used in personal computers.
Japan's big chip makers earlier announced they would scale back investment in microchip production facilities from April.
Rumours have been flying for days that the South Korean government was orchestrating a move by producers to cut output of the most commonly used chips.
However, some Seoul-based analysts said they believed Samsung's strategy went beyond trying to rescue 16-megabit prices, which have plunged by around 80 percent in a year.

They said Samsung would try to use its muscle to push the global market towards 64-megabit chips, a move that could boost its profits and -- if it could could turn markets fast enough -- leave smaller rivals in Taiwan and Japan stranded.
"What I think is going on is that they are shifting to 64-megabit production. What they're really trying to achieve is to push this cross-over," said Matt Cleary, an electronics analyst at HG Asia.
"They're hoping to push quickly so there will be a period when there are a smaller number of producers in the market," Cleary said.
"Korea has been looking to this transition and preparing for this transition for months. Now they're ready."
Samsung said in a statement it had cut production of 16-megabit chips since the end of last year because prices had fallen almost to below a break-even point.
Further price cuts would threaten the global industry and the company would "continue to regulate the poduction volume" until prices rose to a reasonable level, it said.

Computer makers now have little incentive to buy the more powerful memory chips, which cost $50-$60 dollars each against about $7 for the smaller ones. They might have less choice if Samsung and big Japanese producers, notably NEC Corp and Toshiba Corp, altered the balance of their production, analysts said.

"The industry-wide aim is to have a cross-over to 64 megabit chips at as high a price as possible," said Han Ilsuk, an analyst at ING Barings Securities. Han said South Korean producers were looking at a price of $50.
The strategy is risky, since the key to success in the computer chip industry is mass production to achieve economies of scale. Cutting output raises unit costs.
In addition, if the market shifted all manufacturers would be saddled with large inventories of 16-megabit chips.
Han said for South Korea's beleaguered manufacturers it was a devil's choice between "the bad and the worse".

Samsung, NEC and Toshiba stood to gain most since their plans to expand 64-megabit production were well advanced, Han said. "They are farthest along the learning curve. Should the market move into 64 megabit they will benefit," he said.
Taiwanese producers "aren't quite ready yet", nor was LG or South Korea's third big chipmaker, Hyundai Electronics Industries.
"Samsung will be ready for mass production of 64-megabit chips by the second quarter of 1998," said Jon Chong-hwa, an analyst at Hannuri-Salomon Securities.
It was now testing the market with monthly production of around one million units, and this would rise to 10 million per month by the second quarter of 1998, he said.
A spokeswoman for Samsung Electronics said: "We are moving towards 64-megabit chips by increasing investment. We'll try to time mass-production when the market is ready."
Japanese companies were sceptical about the South Korean announcwments.
"There is no way of confirming whether South Korean production cuts will truly take place or not and therefore we cannot comment," said a Toshiba spokesman.
